title: Career attainment can be measured by time to reach a job level, not wages alone
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 34292; database of more than 150 million resumes linked to industry, firm-size category, job titles, wages, education, and transitions
geography: United States labor-market resumes and public-to-private career transitions

observations.period: U.S. career attainment and job-title progression; paper issued 2025

denominator.unit: resumes in the study database, more than

seniority_definition.value: seniority is the number of years it takes the median individual within the same industry and firm-size category to attain a worker's job title

wage_alignment.value: seniority is positively correlated with wages

education_alignment.value: seniority is positively correlated with educational attainment

public_private_transition.value: public-sector individuals with higher seniority levels are more likely to transition to higher-paying private-sector positions

observations.method: The authors construct a non-pecuniary career-attainment measure from the time required to reach job titles in a resume database of more than 150 million records, conditioning the median time on industry and firm size, and test alignment with wages, education, and public-to-private transitions.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract does not observe job quality, control, hours, benefits, health, care, debt, housing, discrimination, promotion opportunity, or why a worker remained or moved. Seniority is a constructed measure of title timing and does not by itself establish career satisfaction, welfare, or causal mobility.
observations.subgroup: Workers represented in the resume database, with a reported public-sector transition analysis; results may vary by industry, firm size, occupation, public agency, demographic group, and resume completeness.
observations.counterinterpretation: Longer time to a title can reflect deliberate non-wage choices, stable work, care, location, or a slower promotion system rather than failure. A higher seniority measure may signal experience or selectivity without guaranteeing better pay, control, or household security. The public-to-private relationship is not proof that seniority causes higher wages.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 34292

boundary: This record adds a career-measurement finding: time to reach a job title contains information not captured by wages alone. It does not establish causal promotion barriers, student-debt effects, job quality, household welfare, discrimination, or that faster title attainment is always better.
